" Having recognized the prowess of that descendant of Raghu, 
I am persuaded that thou art not able to withstand him in 
combat, when even Bali and Namuchi succumbed to him. 
Whether thou dost enter into conflict with him or makest thy 
peace, do not speak his name to me, if thou wouldst see me live! 
" In this world, there are countless virtuous souls engaged 
in the practice of Yoga, fulfilling their every duty, who yet 
perish with those about them through another's fault. I too, 
therefore, should be doomed to die for another's misdeeds ! 
0 Ranger of the Night, do what thou deernest to be right, 
but follow thee I will not. Truly Rama, who is full of zeal, 
courage and prowess, will prove to be the destroyer of the 
titans of this world. Though the wicked-minded Khara of 
J anasthana was slain by him on account of Shurpanakha, 
how, in truth, is he to blame for that ? 
" I have uttered these words for thy good and the good of 
thy kinsmen ; if thou disregardest them, thou and thy people 
will assuredly perish in combat with Rama ! "

RavaM's Wrath 
As one about to die refuses a remedy, so did Ravana repudiate 
Maricha's judicious and opportune words and, having listened 
to this salutory discourse, replied in harsh and ill-considered 
accents, saying :-
" Thou Wretch, what thou hast spoken will bear no fruit, 
as seed that is sown on barren soil comes to nought, nor will 
it alter my determination to enter into combat with Rams, 
who is but a witless and insignificant creature.

"It is proper, when asked, to put forward the advantages 
and disadvantages of a project and what will best serve or

seeking his master's good, will answer with due deference, 
standing before him with joined palms, in words fitting to the

who, having regard to his dignity, is thereby affronted. 
" Kings of limitless power represent the five Gods : Agni, 
Indra, Soma, Yama and Varuna, symbolising ardour, valout, 
gentleness, retribution and forgiveness ; therefore at all times 
they should be honoured and revered. Thou, nevertheless, 
disregarding thy duty, dost only manifest arrogance. Thou to 
whom I have come as a guest hast treated me as a miscreant. 
I have not consulted thee regarding what is expedient or

brief.summary_1line: Ravana angrily rejects Maricha’s warning about Rama and orders him to become a golden deer to lure Rama away so Ravana can abduct Sita.

image_candidates.scene_text: Ravana, furious and regal, stands before Maricha and commands him to transform into a dazzling golden deer to lure Rama away from the hermitage.
A magical golden deer studded with silver appears near Rama’s forest hermitage while Sita gazes at it in wonder.
Ravana boasts in his chariot of his plan to carry off Sita once Rama and Lakshmana are drawn away into the forest.

deep.rich_summary: Maricha warns Ravana that Rama’s power is so terrifying that even hearing syllables beginning with “Ra” fills him with dread, and he predicts disaster if Ravana provokes him. He argues that Rama has already slain mighty demons like Khara and that opposing him will doom the titans. Ravana, enraged, dismisses the counsel and insists on his plan to abduct Sita. He rebukes Maricha for speaking pessimistically and lectures him on obedience to kings, whom he likens to divine powers. Ravana then reveals his scheme: Maricha must transform into a wondrous golden deer to lure Rama away from the hermitage. When Rama pursues it and Lakshmana is drawn away by a deceptive cry, Ravana will seize Sita and carry her to Lanka. The passage marks the decisive plotting that sets the famous abduction in motion.

highlight_spans.why: Sets the setting within the Aranya Kanda, the forest book where the central tragedy of Sita’s abduction unfolds.
Maricha’s fearful confession about Rama’s terrifying reputation shows how even powerful demons dread him.
Ravana declares his intent to abduct Rama’s beloved wife, revealing the central crime that drives the epic’s coming war.
Ravana explains the magical golden deer ruse—one of the most famous deceptions in the Ramayana.
The imitation cry of 'O Sita! O Lakshmana!' foreshadows the emotional manipulation that separates the protectors from Sita.

top_scenes.scene_text: Ravana, blazing with anger, stands before the reluctant Maricha while describing the sinister plan to steal Sita.
Maricha transforming through magic into a radiant golden deer studded with silver, gleaming in the forest near Rama’s hermitage.
The enchanted deer running through the forest as Rama pursues it, while far away a deceptive cry of 'O Sita! O Lakshmana!' echoes through the trees.
